title: How the Bank of England is putting its internal AI tools to work
summary: The Bank of England’s regional Agents gather intelligence from businesses across the UK’s twelve Agencies. Their reports reach the Monetary Policy Committee because people familiar with individual firms can distinguish a recurring change in trading conditions from one company’s exceptional experience. Chief Data Officer Ben Martin describes an application that helps the Agents search this material, identify themes and look for patterns across contacts. The Agents retain responsibility for judging what the evidence means. His 4 November speech sets this example within a wider effort to improve how the Bank collects, shares and analyses information for its monetary and financial stability work (“Equip”).

The starting point is the Enterprise Data Platform. Its core was deployed earlier in the year, and the Bank was moving services onto it in stages. The platform is designed to bring regulatory and statistical returns together with economic and market data under common arrangements for receiving, transforming and reusing information. It also provides analytical tools and approved models. The choice has an institutional rationale. Data collected for one responsibility may answer a question elsewhere in the Bank. Separate systems can obscure that possibility, while a shared platform still requires someone to know where a series came from, which controls apply and what its limitations are. Martin treats migration, quality and governance as continuing work (“Enable”).

He distinguishes tools available to staff generally from applications designed for a particular workflow. Nearly all colleagues use Microsoft 365 Copilot weekly, he reports, and some developers use a coding assistant. Staff have also built agents to answer internal service questions. The bespoke GRACE application gives staff access to trusted internal knowledge through an email interface. Colleagues can send a question, return to their other work, and review the response in a retained email exchange. The Agents’ application, ARIA, instead supports analysis of intelligence gathered through business relationships. Martin’s examples show where a tool enters a decision process. The speech offers no estimate of the accuracy gained, analyst time saved or effect on a policy decision (“Equip”).

The controls Martin describes start with specifying a narrow business purpose. They extend to reliability and data quality, an understanding of the intended use, security, testing of how the technology affects users’ behaviour, ethical standards and the ability to keep performing as conditions change. A tool judged suitable for navigating internal guidance therefore cannot be presumed suitable for interpreting economic intelligence. The reference point is the job a user needs to complete and the consequences of an erroneous answer. Adoption figures reveal the reach of the programme, while assessing those consequences requires evidence from the work itself (“Equip”).

Training and management practices form the other part of the implementation. The Bank’s learning function has delivered more than 250 courses, followed introductory sessions with application-specific teaching and offered clinics for staff using tools in their own roles. A data community of almost 2,000 members supports peer learning. The Bank has also formed a data profession across disciplines, and Martin describes an innovation hub where colleagues can try approaches with support and safeguards. Senior managers are expected to make room for experimentation and a leadership programme was planned. Taken together, these details make the regional Agents example testable. An organisation may have installed an application and taught staff how to operate it. Its contribution ultimately depends on whether staff can identify a useful pattern, challenge an implausible output and explain what evidence supports their judgement (“Equip”, “Empower” and conclusion).

questions.question: Does ARIA identify developments that the regional Agents can verify?
questions.detail: Compare a sample of the application’s themes with the underlying contact records, anonymised where necessary, and the Agents’ assessments recorded before committee briefings. Check coverage across regions, business sizes and sectors. Ask reviewers to record both missed developments and plausible-sounding patterns generated by repeated reports from a small set of contacts.

questions.question: Can an analyst reproduce a published calculation after migration to the enterprise platform?
questions.detail: Select regulatory and economic series used by more than one area of the Bank. Trace their original returns, transformations, revisions, permissions and quality checks through the legacy and new environments. Re-run a fixed historical analysis in both and investigate differences. Count the time needed to explain a discrepancy as well as the number of discrepancies found.

questions.question: Which forms of training change the quality of work?
questions.detail: Compare matched tasks completed before and after an introductory session, a role-specific clinic or participation in the professional community. Use staff work samples, review comments and documented corrections alongside attendance. Assess whether experienced staff can recognise a misleading answer, find the original evidence and explain its limitations. Weekly usage alone cannot establish those capabilities. Check whether these capabilities remain evident in repeat samples several months later.
